On the night the monthly statements job runs, the
table keeps growing, autovacuum runs without removing anything, and at 2 a.m. a routine migration adds a column and the API stops answering. The job only reads: it opens a

transaction "for a consistent view", loads the accounts, and sends one email per account before committing. In a test on PostgreSQL 18 with one such idle transaction open, five rounds of updating 100,000 rows followed by
grew the table from 8,696 kB to 25 MB, and
reported 500,000 rows "dead but not yet removable". Without the idle transaction, the same five rounds kept the table at 8,696 kB.
The belief: a long-running transaction that only reads data doesn't affect anyone else.
It sounds like the whole point of

. PostgreSQL's own introduction says that reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading, and a read-only transaction has nothing to commit and nothing to roll back. Developers coming from SQL Server's default level are used to readers releasing their locks as soon as a statement ends. And the cost is invisible where the code runs: the job finishes, the emails go out, and nothing in its logs mentions bloat or blocked migrations.

Bloat stays after the transaction ends
When the idle transaction in the test ended, the next

marks the space as available for reuse but doesn't return it to the operating system, except for completely empty pages at the end of the table.
